title: Best Dehumidifier for a Cellar (2026): Root & Wine Cellar Picks
h1: The Best Dehumidifiers for Root Cellars and Wine Cellars
dek: A cellar isn't a basement. Before you dry it out, know what's stored down there — your potatoes may want far more humidity than you think.
description: Need a dehumidifier for a root cellar or wine cellar? Find the right humidity target first, then pick a unit with a high-range humidistat or cold-weather design.
intro: Before buying a dehumidifier for a root cellar, figure out what the cellar is for. A traditional root or fruit cellar is designed to stay very humid — University of Missouri Extension recommends **85–95% relative humidity** for most root vegetables — so produce doesn't shrivel. Run it down to a basement's usual 45–55% and you'll dry out your harvest.

That's why many cellar owners actually need a hygrometer and, sometimes, a humidifier more than a dehumidifier. A dehumidifier earns its place when condensation is dripping from the ceiling or puddling after heavy rain — and even then, it should be set high, not low. A wine cellar is a third case, aiming for a cooler, steadier 50–70%.
Below are our picks for diagnosing your cellar, fixing genuine excess moisture without over-drying, handling cold temperatures and treating small cellars with no outlet.
topPicksLead: Start with the **AcuRite 01080M** hygrometer to learn what your cellar really needs; if it's truly too wet, the **Midea Cube 35** is our top dehumidifier because its humidistat goes high enough for a produce cellar.

pros: Shows whether the cellar is too wet or too dry
Easy to read at a glance
Inexpensive insurance before buying a machine
cons: Place it near produce, not the door, for useful readings
products.whyWeLoveIt: Most people assume a damp cellar needs drying. A hygrometer often proves the opposite: a root cellar reading 70% isn't too humid — it's too dry for stored vegetables. Measure before you buy.
products.performance: Put it at shelf height near your produce bins for a day or two, since readings by the stairs or door can differ noticeably from where the food sits. Use it to confirm whether condensation is a real problem and, later, to check your dehumidifier isn't overdoing it.

Large lift-off base tank or hose drainage
cons: Must be set high, against habit
products.whyWeLoveIt: Most basement dehumidifiers top out well below the 80–85% setting a produce cellar needs. The Cube 35's humidistat adjusts in 5% steps up to 85%, so it can knock down dripping condensation without stripping moisture from your vegetables.
products.performance: It's rated at 35 pints a day under the 2019 DOE test — plenty for spring-rain surges across an entire cellar. Set it at 80–85% for a root cellar or around 60% for a wine cellar and let it cycle. Because it's a compressor unit, it works best in cellars that stay above about 41°F. Our [humidistat settings guide](/guides/dehumidifier-humidistat-settings-guide/) explains how to pick a target.

products.whyWeLoveIt: Many cellars spend much of the year between 32°F and 50°F, where a compressor unit spends more time defrosting than drying. A desiccant unit has no cold coil, so it keeps working.
products.performance: Ivation rates it for about 270 square feet and operation down to around 33°F. It's best for trimming excess condensation in a smaller cellar rather than overriding the cellar's natural cooling and ventilation. Pair it with a hygrometer, since desiccant units can dry a space fast. See more in our [desiccant dehumidifier](/best/best-desiccant-dehumidifier/) guide.

Target for drier-storing crops like squash and onions
Typical target for a wine cellar

blocks.text: Temperature matters too. Most cellars run between 32°F and 50°F, and a standard compressor dehumidifier starts icing up below about 41°F — so the type of unit matters as much as the setting.

We don't lab-test. We started from extension-service storage guidance for produce and common wine-storage targets, then compared manufacturer specs for humidistat range, low-temperature operation and coverage. We read owner reviews for recurring issues such as icing, over-drying and inaccurate sensors.
Because most cellars need a high target, the humidistat's upper limit was our top criterion, followed by cold-weather performance and whether the unit needs an outlet.

sections.heading: What to look for in a cellar dehumidifier

items.label: A high humidistat ceiling
items.text: For a root cellar, you need a setting near 80–85%. Many basement units stop at 60–70%.

items.label: Cold-weather performance
items.text: Below about 41°F, choose a desiccant unit. Our [freezing up guide](/guides/dehumidifier-freezing-up/) explains why compressors ice.

items.label: A hygrometer at shelf height
items.text: Measure where the food is, not at the entrance.

items.label: Power availability
items.text: No outlet? A renewable silica unit is your only practical option.

items.label: Real dripping, not just damp
items.text: Cool, earthy-smelling air is normal. Water running down walls or pooling is the true signal.

sections.heading: Root cellar vs. wine cellar: different targets

blocks.text: In a purpose-built wine room, the cooling unit usually manages humidity along with temperature, so check its settings first. In a converted basement cellar, a compressor dehumidifier set around 60% works as long as the room stays above about 41°F; colder cellars call for a desiccant model. Keep a hygrometer near the racks so corks don't dry out.

sections.heading: When a root cellar actually needs a dehumidifier

items: Measure with a hygrometer near the produce for 24–48 hours.
If the reading is below 85% and produce is shriveling, add moisture — not a dehumidifier.
If water is dripping from the ceiling or pooling after rain, check ventilation and drainage first.
If condensation persists, run a dehumidifier set at 80–85%, never at a basement setting.
Recheck the reading weekly and adjust.

blocks.title: Too dry is the more common problem
blocks.text: Soft, wrinkled or sprouting vegetables usually signal a cellar that's too dry. Our [dehumidifier vs. humidifier](/guides/dehumidifier-vs-humidifier/) guide explains how to tell which you need.

sections.heading: Ventilation and storage tips for a healthier cellar

blocks.text: Traditional root cellars rely on a low intake vent and a high exhaust vent to move cool, fresh air through the space. When those vents are blocked, condensation and stale odors build up — and no dehumidifier setting fixes that as well as restoring airflow.

items: **Clear both vents** of leaves, snow and stored items each season.
**Separate apples and pears** from potatoes and carrots; ripening fruit releases ethylene that shortens their storage life.
**Store squash and onions higher up**, where air tends to be warmer and drier, and root vegetables lower down.
**Use slatted shelves and crates** so air can circulate around produce.
**Check for standing water** after storms and fix grading or gutters outside if it recurs.

blocks.text: If musty smells drift from the cellar into the house, our [dehumidifier for musty smell](/best/best-dehumidifier-for-musty-smell/) guide covers tracking down the source.

Start with the **AcuRite 01080M** hygrometer — for many root cellars, the problem turns out to be too little moisture, not too much. If condensation really is dripping, the **Midea Cube 35** is the best pick because its humidistat reaches 85%. The **Ivation 13-Pint Desiccant** takes over in cold cellars, and the **Eva-Dry E-500** handles small cellars with no outlet. For the basement next door, which does want 45–55%, see our [basement dehumidifier](/best/best-dehumidifier-for-basement/) picks.

faqs.q: Does a root cellar need a dehumidifier?
faqs.a: Usually not. Root vegetables keep best at 85–95% relative humidity, so a dehumidifier at a normal home setting will dry out your produce. Use one only for dripping condensation, and set it at 80–85%.

faqs.q: What humidity should a dehumidifier be set to in a root cellar?
faqs.a: Around 80–85%, if the humidistat allows it — high enough to stop dripping without over-drying produce. The Midea Cube's humidistat goes up to 85% in 5% steps.

faqs.q: Do I need a wine cellar dehumidifier?
faqs.a: Only if the cellar sits above about 70% for long periods. Wine cellars generally target 50–70%; a purpose-built cooling unit often handles humidity, while a converted cellar may need a dehumidifier set near 60%.

faqs.q: Will a dehumidifier work in a cold cellar?
faqs.a: A compressor unit loses capacity and ices up below about 41°F. A desiccant unit like the Ivation 13-Pint keeps working down to about 33°F.

faqs.q: How do I know if my cellar is too damp?
faqs.a: Look for water beading on the ceiling, running down walls or pooling after rain. An earthy smell and cool, moist air are normal for a working root cellar.
